source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Manual (hand) harvest is the common method for smallholder corn farmers in Cambodia, and this source describes three variations: (1) harvesting the whole plant and stacking it in the field to dry before husking; (2) harvesting only the ears and leaving the stalks standing or cut in the field; and (3) harvesting ears with the husk removed in the field, then drying the husked ears further before shelling.

Key factors in choosing harvest timing include: grain and cob moisture level (needs to be low enough for the intended storage method), stalk moisture (affects how easily ears separate from the stalk), and confirmation that the crop has finished accumulating dry matter (physiological maturity, see the maturity indicators topic).

In areas with access to farm mechanisation, combine-harvesting is increasingly used, especially on larger commercial fields -- this substantially reduces labour and time compared to hand harvest but requires capital investment or rental access to a machine, which is not available to every farmer.
